abstract: Binary cellular decisions are generally attributed to gene regulatory networks, with cytoskeletal-driven shape changes often treated as an output. Yet, whether the cytoskeleton can itself implement switch-like logic to drive abrupt morphological transitions remains unknown. In the primate amniotic sac, the extraembryonic amnion derives directly from the columnar epiblast and abruptly flattens into a squamous epithelium to form a highly asymmetric cavity. Here, we identify a cytoskeletal switch driving this developmental bifurcation in human gastrula models. Mutual inhibition between actomyosin and keratin networks generates two mechanical attractors: amnion cells flip into a keratin-rich, squamous shape, while the epiblast remains myosin-rich and columnar. Ectopic activation of YAP1-TEAD signaling triggers the myosin-keratin switch without inducing amnion specification, establishing that the switch is not simply a consequence of fate changes. Conversely, preventing the switch disrupts amnion specification, showing that this shape bifurcation gates lineage commitment. Single-cell transcriptomics across cytoskeletal perturbations revealed a transcriptional signature for the toggle switch, which is recapitulated in vivo in the human and marmoset amnion. Together, our findings show that the cytoskeleton acts not only as an effector of tissue shape but as a decision-making module, implementing the same toggle switch logic as gene regulatory networks to drive morphological bifurcations.
